items.title: Why founders keep failing to vibecode their own LLM inference engine
items.summary_1line: Why founders keep failing to vibecode their own LLM inference engine Startup Fortune
items.editor_note: Latest item: opinion-style coverage of failed DIY inference engines; headline-only, no verifiable detail.

editorial.tldr: "Their Own" groups three items that share a phrase, not one developing event. They run from a Oct 14 paper on distilling web agents from black-box teachers to an Oct 21 study of models rewriting their own harness.
editorial.whats_new: A Startup Fortune piece on Oct 24 argues founders keep failing when they try to vibecode their own LLM inference engine; only the headline was available, so its evidence is unverified.
editorial.why_it_matters: All three touch the build-versus-depend question for agent stacks: distill a cheaper agent, let the model tune its own scaffold, or write your own serving layer. None yet gives production evidence.
editorial.take_for_builders: Do not replace a maintained inference server (vLLM, SGLang or a hosted API) with a self-written engine on the strength of this piece; keep the existing stack until a source shows benchmarked results.

status.detail: Three unrelated items sharing a phrase; no single event is unfolding.

open_questions: Do the harness-improvement results on ARC-AGI-3 hold on production agent tasks outside that benchmark?
Does the black-box distillation approach match its closed-model teacher on web-agent success rate at lower inference cost?
Does the Startup Fortune piece name concrete failure modes of self-built inference engines, such as throughput, memory or batching?
